name: Marco Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Look, it starts on my phone before I'm out of bed. The AI feed planner has already worked out the rations for the 300 sows overnight, and the camera in the finishing shed has flagged any pig that's off its weight. My wife Lucia's a vet nurse, so she's gone by seven, and I'm out with Piotr and Jade by half seven. Ridgeway's 160 hectares, pigs outdoors and maize and barley on the rest, so it's pigs in the morning and fields in the afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love trying things. I had a drone spraying the headlands last spring before anyone round here had seen one. What wears me out is the pig price, which goes up and down like a yo-yo, and the hours in winter when the mud's up to your knees. And I worry about Piotr and Jade, because I'm the one who has to make their jobs make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you, it's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd post something on the farm tech forum I'm on, probably a bit disappointed. People round here would rib me for all the gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. The tools I use already save me maybe an hour a day, and that carries on. The farm's in good shape, we've got savings and no big debts, so the pig price is the only thing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the feed planner and the camera, and probably try one or two new apps a year like I do now. I'd keep Piotr and Jade on, same hours. Nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, if I'm honest, because I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that keeps you up, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pig price, always. In 2023 the pig price dropped so far we lost money on every pig for six months. The savings got us through, and that's why I keep them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older son Leo writes software for a bank, so he'd be glad. My younger one, Sam, is a chef. I'd tell Leo his job's safe after all and to stop sending me articles about the end of the world.

say: AI is a good **tool**, not a miracle, like I always said.
I'd post my mild **disappointment** on the farm tech forum.
think: My tools already save me about **an hour a day**, and that carries on.
With **savings and no debts**, only the pig price keeps me up.
do: Keep using the **feed planner** and shed camera.
Try one or two **new apps** a year, as now.
Keep **Piotr and Jade** on the same hours.
feel: **Calm**, and a little let down because he likes **new toys**.
S0.quote: In 2023 the pig price dropped so far we lost money on every pig for six months.
fieldNote: A daily AI user who sees the plateau as a **letdown**, not a relief.
His standing worry is the **pig price**, and the cushion was built for it.
Thinks of his two **workers** before he's asked.

steps.text: Keep using the AI feed planner and shed weight camera daily
Keep Piotr and Jade on at the same hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers should get stuck in and learn it, because the buyers and the feed companies already are. Online I'd say the government needs to fund training for farm workers, not just hand out grants for kit. Kit is easy, it's the people side that gets forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good news. The thinking side of my job, ordering feed, booking the lorry, planning the drilling, the pig movement paperwork, that's maybe a fifth of my week, and AI would take most of it. My hands-on work changes slowly, so I'd have more time in the sheds where I'm actually useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand all the ordering and paperwork to AI tools in the first six months. I'd put about 35,000 into a robot weeder for the maize the moment a decent one is on sale. And I'd sit down with Jade and offer to pay for her to learn the machines, so she runs them instead of being replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It's the version I was hoping for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would feel it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade's 22 and does a lot of the field work by hand. If I buy the weeder, her hoeing hours go, so I'd pay her more to take on the machine. I'd rather Jade learned to run and fix the robot, because otherwise I'm the bloke who bought a machine to replace a young woman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone in the family who'd feel it more than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo, my son at the bank, would feel it more than me in this one. His bank would want fewer coders. I'd tell him to come and talk it through over Sunday lunch, and that he can always stay with us while he works out his next move.

say: Farmers should **learn it now**, because buyers and feed firms already have.
Government should fund **training for workers**, not just grants for kit.
think: About **a fifth** of my week is thinking work, and AI would take most of it.
That frees me for the **sheds**, where I'm actually useful.
do: Hand **ordering and paperwork** to AI tools within six months.
Buy a **35,000 robot weeder** for the maize when one is ready.
Pay for **Jade** to learn to run and fix the machines.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**; it's the version he hoped for.
S1.quote: I'd rather Jade learned to run and fix the robot, because otherwise I'm the bloke who bought a machine to replace a young woman.
fieldNote: Clearly **gains** from this picture and knows it.
His progressive view shows as **duty to his workers**, not opposition to tech.
Notes his son **Leo** in banking software is more exposed than he is.

steps.text: Move feed ordering, lorry bookings and pig paperwork to AI tools
Buy a 35,000 robot weeder for the maize fields
Pay for Jade to train on running and fixing the weeder

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a plan from government, now, not in 2030: retraining money, and some kind of income for people whose work goes. I'd say it on the forum and I'd say it to the farmers' union, who'll think I've gone soft. Two years is nothing when you're talking about whole trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Ridgeway itself, I think we'd do all right. The AI in 2028 takes my paperwork and planning, which I'd welcome, and the robots in 2031 could run most of the sheds and fields. The hard part is that Piotr and Jade's jobs basically vanish in 2031, and when every farm has robots the pig price falls, so the margin I've got now won't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2028 I'd let AI run the planning, the buying and the selling. I'd start pricing robots for the sheds straight away, and I'd budget about 120,000 from savings and the bank for 2031. I'd tell Piotr in writing that I'll pay for a course of his choice from 2029, and keep his wage until he's into something else. And I'd join a campaign for a public retraining fund, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My farm's fine, but I'd be the one telling two good people their jobs are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Piotr?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Piotr's 45 and has been with me eleven years. He's got two teenagers. I'd tell him myself, in the kitchen, with a coffee, not by text. I'd offer him the first job running the robots if he wants it, and the course money if he doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're buying robots and campaigning for the people they replace. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not a contradiction, it's just uncomfortable. I'd buy the robots because my neighbours will, and if I don't, the farm can't compete. I'd still want laws so that everyone who loses work to a machine gets something back from the people who own the machines, including me.

say: We need a **government plan** now: retraining money and income support.
**Two years** is nothing when whole trades are changing.
think: Ridgeway would **do all right**, with AI and robots running most of the work.
**Piotr and Jade's** jobs vanish in 2031, and the pig price falls.
do: Let AI run **planning, buying and selling** from 2028.
Budget about **120,000** for shed robots by 2031.
Pay for **Piotr's course** and join a campaign for a public retraining fund.
feel: **Uneasy**: the farm is fine, but he'd have to tell two people their **jobs are going**.
S2.quote: I'd buy the robots because my neighbours will, and if I don't, the farm can't compete.
fieldNote: Sees the **gap** between AI in 2028 and robots in 2031 as time to prepare his workers.
Holds an **uncomfortable position**: buys robots and campaigns for those they replace.
Plans to tell **Piotr** face to face, in the kitchen, not by text.

steps.text: Hand feed buying, planning and pig sales to AI from 2028
Budget about 120,000 from savings and the bank for shed robots
Join a campaign for a public retraining fund for farm workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get this right if we start today. I'd be the one at the farmers' union saying, let's plan retraining now, before 2031. I'd probably offer Ridgeway as a test farm so people can see the machines working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the timing's almost perfect. The AI arrives in 2031, the robots around 2034, and I'm 66 in 2034. I could set Ridgeway up with the machines and step back to a couple of days a week, and that sounds good to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by trialling a robot for the sheds with the supplier, maybe on a lease, so I know what works before I buy. I'd offer the neighbours my drone and planning setup as a paid service, a few hundred a job. And I'd give Piotr and Jade five years' notice of the plan, so they can choose training on my money while they're still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of me is looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you get your neighbours on board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invite the neighbours round every spring to see what the robots were doing, with bacon rolls. Half of them would come to laugh and half to steal ideas. Farming's always moved that way: you see a new thing over the hedge before you try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would have it harder in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Leo probably. His bank job would go with the AI in 2031, and he's got a mortgage. I'd tell him there's a place at Ridgeway running the systems, and he'd probably turn it down, but the offer would be there.

say: Five years is **enough** if we start today.
I'd offer Ridgeway as a **test farm** so people see the machines working.
think: The timing is **almost perfect**: robots around 2034, when I'm 66.
I could set the farm up and step back to **two days a week**.
do: Lease a **shed robot** on trial before buying.
Sell his drone and planning setup to **neighbours** as a paid service.
Give Piotr and Jade **five years' notice** with paid training.
S3.quote: Farming's always moved that way: you see a new thing over the hedge before you try it.
fieldNote: The five-year warning lines up neatly with his **retirement at 66**.
Sees himself as the **local demonstrator** of new machines.
His worry shifts to his son **Leo**, a coder with a mortgage.

steps.text: Lease a shed robot from the supplier on a trial
Sell drone spraying and AI planning to neighbours for a few hundred a job
Buy the shed robots once the trial works, before 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and the farms that waste it deserve what they get. Then I'd feel bad for saying that, and I'd add that the government should still fund training. I tend to say the second thing a bit late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's after retirement. Robots arrive around 2039, when I'm 71, and I'd have been half-retired for years. The AI in 2036 might still be useful to me for running Ridgeway from the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, adding tools as they come. I'd grow the drone and planning service for neighbours into a proper little business. Piotr would likely retire before the robots, and Jade would have time to retrain on whatever she chooses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, this is the easy one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does retirement look like for you, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Lucia says I'll never retire, I'll just retire into the shed with a laptop. She's probably right. I'd like to be the old man in the village who can fix the robots when they go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would have to think hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade would have the hard choice, because she's the only one young enough to work through it. I'd tell her the tech side will always need people who can talk to farmers. She's good at that, better than me.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and farms that waste it will pay.
The government should still **fund training**, I'd add a bit late.
think: The robots arrive around **2039**, after I've half-retired.
The AI in **2036** could help me run Ridgeway from the kitchen.
do: Keep adding **new tools** as they come.
Grow the **drone and planning** service into a small business.
Leave **Jade** time to retrain on whatever she chooses.
feel: **Calm**; he calls this one the **easy one**.
S4.quote: My wife Lucia says I'll never retire, I'll just retire into the shed with a laptop.
fieldNote: Catches himself being **harsh** and corrects himself, showing his progressive side.
Plans to turn his tech hobby into a **side business** for neighbours.
Sees **Jade** as the one with the real choice to make.

steps.text: Keep adding AI tools at Ridgeway as they come out
Grow the neighbour drone and planning service into a small business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My farm would cope, but Piotr and Jade wouldn't have time, and neither would most farm workers. What would help is a public retraining fund paid for partly by the people who own the machines, me included, and a proper income for anyone whose trade disappears.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'm excited, and I am, a bit. People like me should say we're excited, and then pay our share for the people who lose out.

headlineQuote: People like me should say we're excited, and then pay our share for the people who lose out.
portrait: A 58-year-old **pig and maize** farmer at Ridgeway who uses AI tools every day.
Employs two workers, **Piotr and Jade**, and thinks about them first in every picture.
Sees robots as **good for his farm** and backs taxes and retraining for those who lose out.
Calm in most pictures and **uneasy** in the fastest, because of his workers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his workers and others wouldn't have time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **public retraining fund** paid partly by machine owners, including him.
A proper **income** for anyone whose trade disappears.
